La Marzocco has never chased attention. For nearly a century, their machines have earned it — quietly, consistently, and by hand. Founded in Florence in 1927, the company helped shape modern espresso as we know it. Their designs are at once industrial and intimate, equally at home in a busy café or a minimalist kitchen. In many ways, La Marzocco is more a standard than a brand.

In recent years, that standard found its way into homes. La Marzocco Home was created not to simplify the craft, but to bring it closer. What began as a small shift, professional equipment made available to the domestic barista, has grown into a global offering for people who care deeply about the ritual of coffee. The team behind that growth had spent the last decade building it, one market at a time, and they wanted to document the journey, sharing what worked, what mattered, and what others could carry forward.

Our brief was to create the La Marzocco Home Playbook. Part guide, part retrospective. It needed to serve multiple audiences: internal teams, international partners, executives, and anyone looking to understand how the work gets done. But above all, it needed to feel like La Marzocco — considered, enduring, and quietly confident.

We treated it less like a corporate manual and more like a brand artifact. The book draws from the visual language of travel guides, archival materials, and slow, tactile publishing. A linen-bound cover, rich color palette, and purposeful typography connect the content to La Marzocco’s Italian roots without leaning on nostalgia.

Every section walks the line between function and feeling. There are frameworks, tools, and insights, but also photography that lingers on the small, human details. A machine being unwrapped for the first time. A storefront in Florence catching morning light. A cup, held in quiet celebration. These moments remind readers what the brand is actually in service of.

The result is a book that doesn’t try to sell anything. It simply reflects a way of working and a way of seeing, the same way La Marzocco has always approached its machines. Thoughtfully made. Built to last. And best understood in use.

content.value: RRE has been backing the best since 1994. One of the oldest and most active VC firms in New York, they’ve invested in over 400 companies across the U.S. and Canada. Often as a first check. Their portfolio includes the likes of Binance, Datadog, Palantir, and Ripple. We worked with their core team to update their brand and digital experience.

Most venture firms look the same. Safe sans serif from Google Fonts. Stock photos of handshakes and glass buildings. Overwhelming grids of outdated portfolio logos. The visual language of half-heartedly trying to say they provide more value than money. RRE had a different problem — they were clearly trying to share a different perspective but their retro-inspired identity looked more nostalgic than forward-thinking. The heavily saturated blue and pixelated aesthetic that once felt clever now felt outdated. And their website had devolved into a maze of confusing messaging and dead-end user paths that buried their track record under poor user experience.

We recognized that RRE's longevity wasn't a liability to overcome but their greatest proof point. The insight became clear: success isn't accidental, it's repeatable. RRE doesn't just stumble into good outcomes, they've systematically built repeat success for three decades by putting founders first, seeing around corners, and trusting entrepreneur instincts over market analysis.

The rebrand centers on the concept of “rrepeat success” — the belief that success isn’t something that just happens but can be made to happen again and again despite changing company leaders, economic cycles, technology waves, and market opportunities. We elevated their founder-first ethos with a clear-eyed stance: “We don’t build companies, we build up those who do.”

Visually, we preserved the retro sensibility they requested but elevated it into something more sophisticated. The refined color palette keeps their signature blue while adding classical depth. Our custom dithering effect transforms photography, layering halftone bitmap textures at 30% opacity to merge heritage qualities with technological modernity. We even built a browser-based dithering tool so their team can create on-brand visuals instantly.

The website experience is layered but intuitive with plenty of smart flourishes: an icon system inspired by early computing, bitmapped textures that nod to the internet’s early days, and unexpected graphic details that make the work feel cared for. It was constructed to digitally organize a long history of success. Want to see exited seed investments? No problem, they’re all right here. Need to know areas of investment? Sure, here’s a short list. Interested in the background of a particular investor? Check it out right here.
As a result, RRE looks the part of what they've always been. A successful venture firm with the wisdom and track record to back the next generation of great entrepreneurs.

The world doesn't need another supplement that feels like medicine. Tabs is the mood-boosting chocolate that helps you feel more — more pleasure, more focus, more ease — disguised as a treat you actually want to take. Each square delivers a specific vibe through ingredients like maca, L-theanine, and caffeine, turning functional benefits into genuine indulgence.

Most wellness brands peddle shame in pretty packages. Take this pill because you're not enough. Swallow this powder to fix what's broken. So we asked, what if feeling good wasn't a problem to solve but a pleasure to embrace?

When we met Tabs, they were trapped in a box labeled "sex chocolate." Their aphrodisiac bars had generated viral buzz, but the brand leaned too heavily on raunchy innuendos and AI-generated imagery of intimate couples with extra thumbs. The result felt more like a gas station impulse buy than a premium mood-enhancing product.

We landed on a simple truth during our explorations: people don't want less of anything good. "More vibes, more feelings, more everything" became our mantra. Why choose between productivity and pleasure when you can have both? We worked towards a brand that could grow beyond bedroom benefits into a full spectrum of emotional states.

The visual identity draws unexpected inspiration from vintage cigarette advertisements and matchbooks — that perfect blend of forbidden and familiar. We crafted a lo-fi system that feels both premium and playful, with illustrations that embody the specific mood-boosting properties of each product variant. The imagery is deliberately imperfect, hand-drawn rather than Bezier-curved, capturing the human quality of the emotions Tabs enhances.

For the verbal identity, Tabs understands what you need to elevate your day and delivers it with confidence and charm. Inspired by the effortless allure of Lenny Kravitz and the cool edge of Christopher Walken, Tabs strikes the perfect balance between being coveted and approachable.

The website brings it all together, guiding visitors through an experience that feels less like shopping for supplements and more like browsing a curated collection of moods. Product descriptions elevate everyday moments rather than promising miracle transformations. No crash, no cringe, no compromises. Just chocolate that actually does something.

Morph is building crypto technology that doesn’t feel like crypto at all. Faster, friendlier, and closer to the apps people already use every day. Fresh off their brand refresh, they asked us to create merch that people would actually wear, not just stuff in a drawer.

The goal was bigger than free T-shirts. Morph needed pieces that captured their energy — playful, smart, and ready for anything — while giving the global team something to rally around at upcoming events. They needed gear that makes you part of something special without needing to shout about it.

We pulled references from streetwear, sticker culture, and the lo-fi spirit of early internet art. Our first attempts pushed hard into that playfulness with color spectrums, new typography, and reimagined versions of their 3D mascot. But in searching for the edge, we started drifting from the center.

So we recalibrated. We traded hand-drawn illustrations for halftone versions of their original renders, anchoring everything in familiar territory. We pulled the palette tighter around their signature green, using flashes of yellow, pink, and blue as accents instead of leads. We kept Morphy as a central character, but treated him more like an emblem than a mascot, using pixelation and bitmap treatments to lean into developer-native textures. Typography stayed flexible, using heavy sans-serifs and pixel fonts where it made sense, without forcing an aesthetic just for the sake of it.

The final collection speaks Morph's language fluently. From pixelated "Global Team" long sleeves to bitmapped koala totes, each piece carries a fragment of the world they're building — one that's fast, open, and a little bit mischievous.

Applause is the indie-app studio run by indie-app developers and aficionados. Unlike their competitors who buy apps only to strip them for parts and sell them for profit, Applause stewards their apps with diligence and passion. In a world of bottom-line deals and profit margins, Applause is focused on giving apps the tools to reach their full potential, in order to make lives better for their users. These are the good guys, a company that’s obsessed with the details and respects the hard work of app builders. And they needed a brand that reflected that.

The brand’s visual expression started with a key strategic insight: Applause not only buys successful apps, but thoughtfully cultivates and grows them. If competitors are app warehouses, Applause is the garden in which apps can flourish.

How do you convey to potential indie app devs that you’re one of them? With a visual language that feels both familiar and innovative, like the enduring consumer tech brands. Leading with elements inspired by Apple — like Garamond, its famed font, and streamlined minimalism — every aspect of the brand reflects the sense of honesty and technical aptitude from tech’s early days. But instead of going purely retro, we took those 70s inspired elements and paired them with more modern, contemporary flourishes that made the brand feel fresh and different. Like the brand’s new mark — an homage to IBM’s resilient and renowned 8-bar logo — every aspect of Applause’s new look communicated a reverence for technology and an ethos for innovation.

Early tech colors, like royal blue, black and white, were also rethought through modern, bold imagery. Apple’s famed negative photo treatments were approached with a new kind of attitude, and paired with additional photo elements made with Studio Freight’s open-sourced ASCII Texture. Illustrations took inspiration from the 8-bit style of the 70s, but were instead applied to lush, organic imagery of unbridled growth.

The result was an incredibly thoughtful, laser-focused brand without frills or excess (just like the apps in Applause’s portfolio), but that doesn’t mean there wasn’t room for playfulness. On the website, we included moments and easter eggs that gave a wink to other indie-app die-hards, like corner radiuses that match the same ones Apple uses in its app store. From each click to every intentionally placed design element, the experience is purposefully referential, but purely, and totally, Applause.

Bullpen lives where crypto actually happens — in Telegram threads, X replies, and unhinged trading channels. As the social-first platform for multiplayer trading, Bullpen makes it effortlessly fun to follow smart money and stay ahead of the market. We teamed up with the Bullpen team to rebrand and update their digital presence.

When they came to us, the product was smart but the brand energy was… off. It felt overly masculine, visually uninspired, and even a bit scammy. Bullpen isn’t for hedge fund suits or DeFi purists. It’s for the 2 a.m. trade warriors making high-risk moves from a cracked iPhone with six tabs open. Their world is chaotic, irreverent, and full of memes, inside jokes, sarcasm, and extreme mood swings. We saw an opportunity to build a brand that speaks their language rather than sanitizing it.

The culture was already writing the brand. It was in the chat threads: the oddball usernames, the hyper-online spellings, the old-school emoticons, the rollercoaster of moods. We turned those into design elements, using the chat bubble as a visual motif. Inside the bubbles, we mirrored the emotional whiplash of trading, from manic glee to full existential meltdown, often within minutes.

The old logomark was an overly-detailed bull’s head, making it clunky and hard to read at the size of tiny Telegram avatars and low-res screenshots. We stripped it down to just the forward-leaning horns. It reads fast, even when it’s small, and signals movement. It still says “bull,” but in a way that you can grab onto without overthinking it.

The typeface, ABC Favorit, does a lot of heavy lifting. High x-height, tight spacing, solid personality. It’s built for interfaces but doesn’t feel cold. We pushed it to heavier weights to give the brand more punch, without tipping into tech-bro territory. The color palette went the opposite direction. We kept it minimal: a punchy bluish-green, a near-black offshoot, and a pale, almost-white tint of the same. Tight and controlled. Strong enough to carry the brand, quiet enough to let the content breathe. An extended set supports the product UI without muddying the brand core.

Yeah, we added a mascot, a slightly ridiculous yet likable cartoon bull. It’s a nod to the weirdness of the space. It’s just fun. Bullpen is serious about what it does, but not so serious that it can’t laugh at itself. To round out the system, we designed a sticker set full of crypto-flavored references — “gm”s, arrows, buy buttons, all of it. They bring extra expression into chat threads, social posts, and user comms. Because half of the brand is context, and Bullpen’s context is extremely online.

All in all, the new Bullpen brand shows up like a native. It matches the energy of the people who actually use it. It’s not cleaned up, dumbed down, or corporate-safe. It’s just here for a good, smart time — and ready to ride the next market swing, wherever it goes.

AI progress faces a fundamental barrier and threat. The computing power needed to train and run models remains concentrated in the hands of tech giants, creating an uneven playing field. Hyperbolic set out to change this with a remarkably simple idea — aggregate idle GPUs from around the world and make them accessible to anyone building with AI.

When Hyperbolic came to us, their team and vision showed promise bordering on revelatory. But their brand promise amounted to little. They looked like countless other developer-focused upstart startups with dark interfaces and technical language that failed to communicate their true value.

We discovered a critical insight during our work together: “Open source does not mean open access.” Having permission to use something means little when you lack the resources to use it. Hyperbolic's platform solves this problem by connecting computing resources with everyone who needs them, from major research institutions, like Stanford and NYU, to independent developers working from home.

The rebrand focused on the clear-eyed conviction that the future of AI should be collaborative. Not gate-kept or deceptively labeled as open. While competitors embraced technical aesthetics they assumed would appeal to insiders, we designed Hyperbolic to look and feel like infrastructure already trusted by the world’s leading enterprises. We designed it to be “The Open Access AI Cloud” providing computing for all.

Every element of the design system serves this vision. The hyperboloid monogram forms a stylized "H" representing boundless potential. The typography combines Acid Grotesk for headlines, KH Teka for body copy, and Diatype Mono for technical elements. The result feels distinctly AI-native without careening into sci-fi. The graphic system includes detailed 3D renders of GPU devices paired with matching line-art illustrations. This duality reinforces the core concept of physical computing hardware made digitally accessible to all. Supporting elements follow minimalist principles with gridded graphics inspired by hyperbolic curves and GPU nodes.

Despite the literal genius of the founders — the CEO completed his Berkeley PhD in record time, the fastest in history, and the CTO regularly exchanges ideas with industry leaders like Andrej Karpathy — we declined working with them multiple times, believing they were too early. But they were remarkably persistent.

That persistence has paid off. Mere months after launching the brand and website, Hyperbolic has grown from a ten-person startup to a serious contender. Over 165,000 developers now use the platform. Their inference service has processed more than 32 billion tokens. Over 3,600 GPU rentals have powered AI workloads around the world. And more than 65,000 compute hours have been delivered — a number accelerating by the hour.

content.value: Brex, a leader in financial management solutions, sought to create a distinct sub-brand for their latest AI advancements. The new Brex AI brand would be unveiled at Brex’s industry event. They tapped Studio Freight to develop a sub-identity that differentiated their product and would leave a lasting impression on attendees.

Our design philosophy was simple: highlight the seamless integration of AI within Brex's financial ecosystem while staying true to the brand's values and commitment. We envisioned a visual identity that set Brex apart in a competitive field and celebrated the harmony between frontier technology and human-centric finance.

In respecting color theory and Brex's existing brand, we chose a complementary shade of blue to harmonize with Brex's orange hue. This vibrant blue injected energy into the event branding, adapting seamlessly to both digital and physical environments with dark and light mode options.

Working with Brex's custom version of Inter, we opted for lighter weights and a unique type scale to evoke inspiration. We also integrated Space Mono for a tech-oriented feel, aligning with Brex's position as a leader in financial innovation.

Drawing on the concept of harmony between Brex's platform, customers, and AI, we crafted 3D renders reminiscent of the unfolding of flowers. This metaphorical depiction showcases the relationship within Brex's ecosystem, even when invisible to the naked eye.

To simplify complex ideas, we introduced illustrations conveying abstract concepts in spend management. These visuals, inspired by our 3D renders, resonated with both technical and non-technical audiences, narrating the journey of problem-solving and solution implementation.
The sub-brand compliments Brex's core system, signaling a new era at the intersection of finance and technology.

At the event, held in San Francisco, the sub-brand provided a platform for Brex's founders and CEO to engage with industry leaders (Google, Sequoia Capital, Morgan Stanely, and more). Through immersive branding experiences and compelling narratives, the event solidifies Brex's pioneering role in AI implementation within fintech.

We ride together. We die together. The Bad Boys franchise cemented Will Smith as an action movie star, so we were honored to create the website and limited-edition merchandise for the Official Bad Boys Movie Store as a celebration of the 25th Anniversary.

In gearing up for Fabtech, one of the premier events in the fabrication and automation industries, Path Robotics tapped Studio Freight to help announce their most groundbreaking release yet — the AF-1. This autonomous welding robot combines advanced computer vision with AI-driven autonomy to deliver unmatched precision and performance in finish welding.

We built the AF-1 visual identity to fit within the existing Path Robotics brand system. To ensure the AF-1 stood out among hundreds of the most competitive innovators in the world, the project included 3D renders, illustrations, and motion design to be used across promotional materials, event installations, merchandise, and the website.

The result was a immersive experience, enabling Path Robotics engage with a bevy of curious prospects and establish the AF-1 as their latest milestone in realizing a future of truly autonomous welding.

content.value: Can AI truly become a public good? 0G thinks so. With its data storage and availability infrastructure, developers can now bring AI on-chain in a highly scalable and secure manner without the previous performance loss experienced on centralized systems — a game changer.

While their team had built remarkable technology, their website wasn’t fully conveying the cutting-edge aspect of their project. And the messaging, bogged down in jargon, was missing critical opportunities to clearly articulate 0G’s groundbreaking technology. If they were revolutionizing AI, they needed a digital expression of their brand with equal ambition. We began by establishing a strong strategic foundation, auditing their existing visual and verbal elements, and conducting an archetype exercise that allowed us to get laser-focused on who they were as a brand.

We noticed that their competitors were focused on owning specific colors. Instead of fighting for territory, we developed a prismatic color system — rich, vibrant, kaleidoscopic — where a dynamic range of colors could be used both individually and as gradients. Cool blues and purples supported more information-heavy moments, like data visualization. Warmer reds and yellows were reserved for moments of innovation, like product features.

Tighter rules were assigned around type, from hierarchy to scale, to elevate the messaging and improve digital way-finding. The illustrations, integral in showcasing the specific aspects of 0G’s technology, were given fresh dimensionality that honored the complex, sophisticated nature of 0G’s work. And the panda mascot? No notes. He was already perfect.

Mercury is the modern banking solution favored by many oft-overlooked startups. In the midst of fast growth, we worked alongside the Mercury team to evolve how they present themselves across various communication channels, bringing depth and versatility to the brand with a non-mercurial design approach that allows them to say more, with less effort.

To accomplish this, our task was to unify the visual representation of Mercury’s platform and products — in both 2D and 3D — for applications across campaigns, web properties, and content marketing. The outcome was a comprehensive library of assets for immediate use, and guidance for creating more well into the future.

We began with defining how the system could harmoniously contain a spectrum of styles and dimensions. For 3D, we explored how materials, colors, lighting, and composition could be updated without straying beyond their existing brand system. Drawing inspiration from classical sculpture, we worked with materials like marble — which have a sense of timeless strength — and balanced them with contemporary resins and polished metals to introduce a modern touch of color. We reinterpreted product interfaces and benefit concepts in 3D, with and without motion. Alongside production, we explore the art direction for 2D applications, so they could inform each other and work together as a final system.

Next, we rebuilt the product visualization suite to be an intuitive, modular system that could flex in representing a wide range of product features, interfaces, and capabilities. Each visual was built with versions in 2D and 3D, as well as intermediate versions where shadows and perspectives were composed to give dimensionality to 2D assets. We kept the color palette for these illustrations minimal, using neutral colors paired with a distinctly-Mercury, twilight-inspired gradient called Dusk.

For editorial illustrations, we sought to abstract important financial concepts into artful compositions — individually distinct yet collectively consistent. Once we landed on the art direction, we made a playbook explaining how foreground, background, and supporting details can be produced, in order, to create a multitude of new illustrations.

Our collaborative efforts were put to the test during the collaboration when Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) suddenly collapsed and fears of a broader run on the banks reached a fever pitch. In the span of a day, they launched and promoted their Mercury Vault offering, which offered FDIC insured accounts up to $5M (instead of the standard $250K), with the support of the new system and assets across digital and campaign applications. Why wait when you can get a win right away?

content.value: zkPass is building the infrastructure to let people prove who they are, without revealing more than they need to. It’s cryptographic privacy for the internet age, enabling anyone to verify sensitive data like identity, credentials, or financials on-chain, without handing that data over. Think of it as a bridge between Web2 and Web3 that doesn’t leak anything in transit.

Our job was to translate that mission into a visual identity and website that felt as advanced as the tech behind it. The challenge was twofold: the category is dense and hard to explain, and it’s also visually crowded with sameness. We built a design system rooted in cryptography — a modular set of symbols, layouts, and type that reference anonymity without defaulting to clichés. The aesthetic is raw and technical by design, striking a balance between structure and ambiguity.

The result is a brand that feels as secure and flexible as the protocol itself. The identity works like a visual proof system — composable, precise, and quietly expressive. On the website, that system comes to life through an immersive interface with layered animations and interactive elements. It’s not just a facelift. It’s a frontend for the future of private, verifiable data.

Clyde is the ownership enrichment platform that unifies (and beautifies) warranty, registration, and issue resolution channels into a single dashboard. Now brands can know, keep, support, and monetize their customers like never before — and unlock the customer lifetime value of their dreams. We worked with the Clyde team to imagine a brand experience where the products we love are capable of loving us back.

content.value: The universal adoption of blockchain technology has been foiled by a core issue — they’re siloed. Siloed blockchains severely limit the audiences, capabilities, and functionalities that developers can access, and diminish the user experience quality their applications can achieve.

Evmos solves this by combining EVM compatibility with cross-chain connectivity. Now it’s possible to build with the depth, familiarity, and developer-friendliness of Ethereum (EVM) and the breadth, interoperability, and freedom of Cosmos.

They have a highly technical offering and vision, so we first focused on making Evmos make sense. The idea of astrogation, a fictional term for safely navigating space, was a north star for how we thought about the brand experience.

We drew on themes from the worlds of Ethereum and Cosmos to create a familiar yet novel sensibility. Because technical company requires demands significant reading, we created custom type as a key distinction. Ultimately, we developed a digital-first brand system capable of keeping their big vision, expanding ecosystem, and growing feature set in orbit.
The crypto landscape can be a tumultuous and unforgiving place with fast-changing market sentiments. Soaring today, crashed tomorrow.

Evmos has a loyal community with deep affinity for the brand, and a governance cohort, so we needed to honor what they loved while moving the brand forward. Evmos also has a vocal crowd of eager critics.

We launched the new brand and website as Evmos 2.0 to indicate that while the vision is the same, there’s new leadership, new possibilities, and new expectations. The reception has been exceedingly positive, from the community and critics alike.
